traveler: Robert Maxwell (born Jan Ludvik Hyman Binyamin Hoch)
title: The Salt Village to the Mount of Olives: Hoch, du Maurier, Maxwell, and the Hole in the Books
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Salt Village and the Road West

stops.name: Solotvyno, the salt village
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell')
stops.campa: In a Carpathian village that mines salt and prays in Yiddish, an Orthodox Jewish family has a son and names him Jan Ludvik Hyman Binyamin Hoch. The place is called Slatinske Doly and belongs to Czechoslovakia; within his lifetime it will belong to Hungary, then the Soviet Union, then Ukraine, and answer to the name Solotvyno. The family is poor. He will change his name several times before he is thirty, and this first one is the only one the village ever knows him by.
suggested_refs: The salt workings of Slatinske Doly / Solotvyno, Carpathian Ruthenia, and its interwar Jewish community

stops.name: Budapest, the boy sent away
stops.date_confidence: [R] reconstruction: the year is a default to January of an approximate date, and the journey to Budapest is not stated in the Wikipedia article this file otherwise follows. Later profiles carry it; no source reached here attests it. The Auschwitz deaths of his family in 1944 are attested.
stops.campa: Germany takes Czechoslovakia apart and the region passes to Hungary. He is about fifteen. Every later profile has his parents putting him on a road out of the village toward Budapest, though the Wikipedia article otherwise relied on does not say so. What is documented is the outcome. He goes west; they do not. After the German occupation of Hungary in 1944 most of his immediate family are murdered at Auschwitz, and he is not told for years. The village goes on mining salt under three more flags.
suggested_refs: Deportation records of the Maramures and Carpathian Ruthenian Jewish communities, spring 1944

stops.name: Marseille, the army in exile
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); the day is defaulted
stops.campa: In the Vieux-Port he joins the Czechoslovak Army in exile, one of thousands of refugees and volunteers gathering in the unoccupied southern ports of a France that has weeks left to give them. He is sixteen years old and speaks no English. Within a month the country he has just enlisted in falls, and the exile army must evacuate a second time, to Britain. He sails with it. The continent he was born on is behind him now, and he will not stand on it again for four years.
suggested_refs: Recruitment registers of the Czechoslovak Army in exile at Marseille and Agde, 1940

stops.name: Cholmondeley Park, the camp in Cheshire
stops.date_confidence: [R] for the camp: Cholmondeley Park was the Czechoslovak army camp in England in 1940, but no source reached places Maxwell there personally. The units and the aliases are [A] (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'). Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The Czechoslovak forces reconstitute on English soil, and their camp in the Cheshire parkland of Cholmondeley is where the refugees are counted and retrained. He leaves them for the British Army and its Royal Pioneer Corps, the labour corps into which foreign volunteers are commonly funnelled, and in 1943 transfers again into the North Staffordshire Regiment as an infantryman. He serves under assumed names, Ivan du Maurier and then Leslie du Maurier. The Hoch of the salt village is already gone.
suggested_refs: The Czechoslovak army camp at Cholmondeley Park, Cheshire, 1940; British Army service records under the du Maurier aliases

segments.name: The Cross and the New Name

stops.name: Gold Beach, the crossing to Normandy
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the regiment's Normandy service is attested; the beach and the day of his own landing are not documented in any source reached. This pin marks the British sector, not a documented footprint. Month defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: The North Staffordshire Regiment crosses to France in the Normandy invasion and lands in the British sector west of Arromanches. Which beach carried him and on what day are not recorded in any source reached. He is twenty-one, a sergeant, fighting his way back toward the continent he was born on with an English regiment and a French name he made up. Four years earlier he had gone the other way across this same water, in a beaten army, with nothing.
suggested_refs: War diaries of the North Staffordshire Regiment, Normandy campaign, June 1944

stops.name: The Maas front, the machine-gun nest
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the action, the month and Montgomery's presentation; [R] for the place. The town is undocumented in every source reached, and this pin marks the 21st Army Group line of January 1945 rather than a named site. An earlier draft of this research placed it at 51.6, 6.1, east of the Rhine, which the army did not reach until March 1945; that coordinate is rejected as anachronistic.
stops.campa: Somewhere on the winter front between the Maas and the German border he storms a machine-gun nest, and for it he is awarded the Military Cross. Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery pins it on him himself. The town is not recorded in any source reached here. By the end of the year he is commissioned captain, five years after coming ashore in Britain as a refugee with no English and a Czechoslovak enlistment number. The naturalization papers are still eighteen months away.
suggested_refs: The London Gazette citation for the Military Cross, January 1945

stops.name: Paris, the marriage to Elisabeth Meynard
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the year and the marriage; [R] for the place and the month. The atlas canonical Paris pin is inherited here because the marriage to a Frenchwoman in 1945 is attested and no source reached names the town or the date.
stops.campa: He marries Elisabeth Meynard, a French Protestant, in the last spring of the war, a soldier of no settled nationality marrying into a country that has just been given back to itself. They will have nine children. She will bury two of them, take an Oxford degree in modern languages at fifty-three, add a doctorate in French literature at sixty with a thesis on the art of letter writing in France, and forty-nine years after this wedding publish the account of the marriage from inside it.
suggested_refs: Elisabeth Maxwell, A Mind of My Own: My Life with Robert Maxwell (1994)

stops.name: Berlin, the press section
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1945-1947 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Discharged from combat into occupation duty, he is posted to Berlin and works in the press section of the Foreign Office in the ruined capital. He is there two years, in the one European city where paper, printing licences and the ownership of scientific journals all pass through Allied hands, and where a captain with fluent German and no English social position can be very useful to people who have lost everything but their copyrights. Pergamon Press is four years away.
suggested_refs: Records of the British Control Commission press and information section, Berlin, 1945-1947

stops.name: London, the deed poll
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for both the naturalization (19 June 1946) and the deed poll (30 June 1948); the atlas canonical London pin stands for an address no source reached specifies
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of June 1946 he is naturalized a British subject. Two years later, on the thirtieth of June 1948, he changes his name by deed poll to Ian Robert Maxwell. Jan Ludvik Hoch of Slatinske Doly is thereby extinguished in English law, having already served under two du Mauriers and a Czechoslovak enlistment number. He is twenty-five, married, decorated, British, and named after nothing in particular. The accent stays with him for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The 1948 deed poll enrolment, Supreme Court of Judicature, changing Hoch to Ian Robert Maxwell

segments.name: Pergamon and the House on the Hill

stops.name: Fitzroy Square, Pergamon Press
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'; Wikipedia, 'Pergamon Press'); month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He buys three quarters of a small scientific publisher called Butterworth-Springer and renames it Pergamon Press. The business is journals: subscriptions libraries cannot cancel, editors who work unpaid for prestige, prices that rise every year because no competing copy of the article exists anywhere on earth. Almost nobody outside the trade has yet noticed what the model can be made to do. Everything else he ever owns is bought with what Pergamon earns.
stops.quote: I tried having male assistants at first [...] But it didn't work. They tend to be too independent; men like to have individuality. Women can become an extension of the boss. They don't mind working overtime, they are more loyal and they can take criticism better. [...] Women are also more efficient than men. I want perfection, and I do my best to get it—so I have trained them myself.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Robert Maxwell, interviewed by Stella King, 'Men Talking About Women,' The Times (London), 23 October 1968, p. 8; quoted in Wikiquote, where this passage stands as an unsourced bullet. The Times archive page is paywalled and the primary text was not verified.
suggested_refs: The Pergamon Press journal list of the 1950s and 1960s

stops.name: Oxford, the death of Karine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); month, day and the Oxford location are defaults, not documented
stops.campa: His daughter Karine dies of leukaemia at three years old. She is the first of the nine children of the marriage to be buried, and the household absorbs it as the household absorbs everything, by not stopping. Pergamon is six years old and growing. Four years after this a car crash will put his eldest son into a coma that lasts until 1968, and the second grave will be dug then. Elisabeth writes about these years long afterwards. He never writes about them at all.
suggested_refs: Elisabeth Maxwell, A Mind of My Own (1994), on the deaths of Karine and Michael

stops.name: Headington Hill Hall, the best council house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the tenancy and the Pergamon relocation; month and day defaulted. The remark quoted below is undated and has no primary transcript.
stops.campa: Pergamon moves out of London to a dilapidated Victorian mansion on a hill above Oxford, owned by the city council, and he rents it as both company headquarters and family home. He restores it. He will live in it for thirty-two years, running a private empire out of a house he does not own from a landlord that is a municipal authority. Editors, ministers, Soviet officials and his own children all come up the same drive. The joke he makes about the arrangement outlives most of the businesses.
stops.quote_source: Robert Maxwell on Headington Hill Hall, undated; Wikipedia encloses only these four words, with 'in the country' outside the quotation. The underlying local-history source (headington.org.uk) renders the whole remark as reported speech with no quotation marks. No primary transcript exists.
suggested_refs: Headington Hill Hall, Oxford, leased from Oxford City Council 1959-1991

stops.name: Maisons-Laffitte, the birth of Ghislaine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year and the place (Wikipedia, 'Ghislaine Maxwell'); month and day defaulted
stops.campa: His ninth and last child is born in the Paris suburb of Maisons-Laffitte and named Ghislaine. She is the one he keeps closest. He will name a yacht after her, and thirty years later that yacht is where he is last seen alive. In July 2020 she is arrested on sex trafficking charges connected to Jeffrey Epstein; in December 2021 she is convicted; in June 2022 she is sentenced to twenty years. Her father has then been dead for thirty-one years, and the arrest reopens him.
suggested_refs: Maisons-Laffitte, Seine-et-Oise, birthplace of Ghislaine Maxwell, 1961

stops.name: Headington Hill Hall, the second grave
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of death and to the 1961 crash (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); month and day defaulted
stops.campa: His son Michael dies of the injuries he took in a car crash seven years earlier, having spent the interval unconscious. He was a schoolboy when the car went off the road and a grown man when he stopped breathing. The father is at this point a Member of Parliament, a publisher with a global list, and a man one year away from losing control of the company he built. Two of the nine are now buried. The house on the hill goes on being the office as well as the home.
suggested_refs: Elisabeth Maxwell, A Mind of My Own (1994), on Michael Maxwell's seven years in coma

segments.name: The Member for Buckingham and the Inspectors

stops.name: Buckingham, the seat won
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell')
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of October he takes Buckingham for Labour, a market-town constituency of farms and commuter villages. The candidate is a Czechoslovak Jewish refugee with a Military Cross and a scientific publishing house, standing for Harold Wilson's party in a seat that has no obvious reason to want him. He wins it twice. He holds surgeries and campaigns hard, and for six years the man who will be remembered as a pirate is a backbench MP with a casework file.
suggested_refs: Buckingham constituency results, general elections of 1964, 1966, 1970 and both of 1974

stops.name: Palace of Westminster, the impatient member
stops.date_confidence: the interview date is attested by the citation carried on Wikiquote, though that citation is formally attached to a different bullet on the same page; the primary Times text was not read
stops.campa: He does not take to the Commons and the Commons does not take to him. In an October interview for The Times he says so himself, in a series on how men talk about women that he uses mostly to talk about himself: the procedure is archaic, the members were unfriendly, he was brash and knows it. The chamber runs on precedence and patience and he has neither. The same interview produces two sentences about women and work that will be quoted against him for the rest of the century.
stops.quote: I can't get on with men [...] or perhaps it might be truer to say that they can't get on with me. They were not very friendly in the Commons, I suppose it was because I was a bit brash; in fact I know I was. I was impatient with the slow archaic procedure.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Robert Maxwell, interviewed by Stella King, 'Men Talking About Women,' The Times (London), 23 October 1968, p. 8; quoted in Wikiquote as an unsourced bullet. The Times archive page is paywalled and the primary text was not verified.
suggested_refs: Stella King, 'Men Talking About Women,' The Times, 23 October 1968, p. 8

stops.name: Bouverie Street, the paper lost to Murdoch
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the failed bid and to October 1969 for the loss of Pergamon; the Bouverie Street coordinate is the News of the World office, approximate, and no source reached places him there
stops.campa: He bids for the News of the World, then the biggest-selling English-language newspaper in the world, and the board rejects him in favour of an Australian few in Fleet Street have yet heard of, Rupert Murdoch. It is the first collision of the two men and it fixes their order for the next twenty years. In the same year Saul Steinberg's Leasco moves on Pergamon, the accounts are opened to outside eyes for the first time, and by October he has been voted out of the company he founded.
suggested_refs: The 1969 News of the World takeover contest; the Leasco bid for Pergamon Press

stops.name: Buckingham, the seat lost
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the day is the 1970 general election polling day
stops.campa: The Conservative William Benyon takes Buckingham from him. He will contest it twice more in 1974 and lose both times, and that is the end of a parliamentary career that produced one memorable interview and no legislation. Eighteen months after this defeat, government inspectors publish a judgment on his fitness to run a public company that follows him for the remaining twenty years of his life. In 1979 the country elects the woman he had said in print it never would.
stops.quote: Britain will never have a woman Prime Minister because women are frightened to take on supreme power.
stops.quote_source: Robert Maxwell, interviewed by Stella King, 'Men Talking About Women,' The Times (London), 23 October 1968, p. 8; this is the one bullet on Wikiquote's Robert Maxwell page carrying an explicit page citation.
suggested_refs: Buckingham constituency result, 18 June 1970

stops.name: Vaduz, the foundation in Liechtenstein
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); month and day are defaults, and Vaduz stands for the principality rather than a documented registered office
stops.campa: He establishes the Maxwell Foundation in Liechtenstein, a jurisdiction whose entire commercial proposition is that the beneficial owner of a legal entity need not be discoverable. It is set up in the same season he is being examined by British inspectors and driven out of his own company. Two decades later, when the money is looked for, the trail runs into structures of this kind and stops. The foundation is lawful, and its function is that nobody outside it can see through it.
suggested_refs: The Maxwell Foundation, Liechtenstein, established 1970

stops.name: Whitehall, the inspectors' verdict
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; month and day defaulted, and the coordinate stands for the department rather than a documented room
stops.campa: Inspectors appointed by the Board of Trade report on the affairs of the International Learning Systems Corporation and, in interim, on Pergamon Press, and reach a sentence that will be quoted in every obituary he ever gets. They acknowledge his abilities and his energy. They then conclude that he is not, in their opinion, a person who can be relied on to exercise proper stewardship of a publicly quoted company. He is forty-seven, out of Parliament, out of Pergamon, and publicly declared unfit.
stops.quote: We regret having to conclude that, notwithstanding Mr Maxwell's acknowledged abilities and energy, he is not in our opinion a person who can be relied on to exercise proper stewardship of a publicly quoted company.
stops.quote_source: R. O. C. Stable and Sir Ronald Leach, Report on the Affairs of the International Learning Systems Corporation Limited: And Interim Report on the Affairs of Pergamon Press Limited (London: H.M. Stationery Office, 1971), as cited on Wikipedia. The HMSO original is not freely available online and was not read; the widely circulated variant 'relied upon' is the corrupt form.
suggested_refs: The 1971 HMSO inspectors' report on ILSC and Pergamon Press
sources: Stable and Leach, HMSO 1971 (cited, not read)

stops.name: Oxford, Pergamon taken back
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the reacquisition, the two lost elections and Elisabeth Maxwell's BA; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Three years after the verdict he buys back control of Pergamon Press, and the company the inspectors said he could not be trusted with is his again. In the same year he loses Buckingham twice more, in February and October, and his wife Elisabeth takes a degree in modern languages at St Hugh's College at fifty-three, having begun studying while the household was in ruins. He is barred from nothing. The report was a judgment and not a disqualification, and English law asked no more of him.
suggested_refs: Elisabeth Maxwell's BA, St Hugh's College, Oxford, 1974; her 1981 doctorate, 'The Art of Letter Writing in France, 1789-1830'

stops.name: London, the printing corporation taken
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); month and day defaulted, and the canonical London pin stands for a corporate address no source reached specifies
stops.campa: He buys the British Printing Corporation, a badly run giant of the British printing trade, and breaks the print unions inside it. It becomes the British Printing and Communication Corporation, then the Maxwell Communication Corporation, and it is the vehicle through which everything afterwards is bought. He is fifty-eight and has spent a decade in the wilderness holding a scientific publisher. From here the acquisitions come annually, and the borrowing that funds them is never fully visible from outside.
suggested_refs: The 1981 acquisition of the British Printing Corporation

stops.name: Holborn Circus, the Mirror bought
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); the day is a default within July 1984
stops.campa: He pays Reed International 113 million pounds for Mirror Group Newspapers and walks into the building at Holborn Circus owning the Daily Mirror, the Sunday Mirror, the Sunday People and the Scottish titles. It is the Labour paper of the British working class and he is now its proprietor. He promises the journalists they will be left free to produce the news, and then puts his own photograph on the front page. The pension funds of this company are the ones he will empty.
stops.quote: free to produce the news without interference
stops.quote_source: Robert Maxwell, press conference on acquiring Mirror Group Newspapers, 1984, as summarized on Wikipedia's 'Robert Maxwell'. Returned by an automated fetch of the article rather than read in a primary transcript; verbatim accuracy is not independently confirmed.
suggested_refs: Mirror Group Newspapers, Holborn Circus, London, acquired July 1984

stops.name: London, the crook and the liar
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year and the occasion, a meeting of Maxwell's new employees at the 1984 takeover; the day is a default and the room is not named in any source reached
stops.campa: At a meeting of the employees he has just acquired, the Mirror journalist Joe Haines stands up and says he can prove their new proprietor is a crook and a liar. Haines is a former press secretary to Harold Wilson and he is opposing the takeover. Within a few years he is working for Maxwell and writing the authorised biography, published in 1988 and largely sympathetic. The hostile book comes after the funeral. Both are by the same man; only one was written while the subject could sue.
stops.quote_source: Joe Haines at a meeting of Maxwell's new Mirror Group employees, 1984, as reported on Wikipedia citing 'Say It Ain't So, Joe', The Spectator, 22 February 1992, p. 15. The Spectator page is subscription-gated and its body text was not retrieved.
suggested_refs: Joe Haines, Maxwell (1988), the authorised biography

stops.name: Makkum, the Lady Ghislaine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year and the yard (Amels of Makkum, Friesland, to a Jon Bannenberg design); month and day defaulted. An earlier draft of this research placed the naming ceremony at an unnamed Dutch yard near Amsterdam, about 120 km wrong; that placement is rejected.
stops.campa: At the Amels yard in the Frisian town of Makkum he commissions a yacht to a Jon Bannenberg design and names it Lady Ghislaine after his youngest daughter, who is brought to the naming. It is his first superyacht. He will use it as a floating office and as a place to be unreachable, and on the fifth of November 1991 it will be the last thing he stands on. The name he gives the boat here is the name that will be running on front pages in 2021, attached to a different trial.
suggested_refs: Amels shipyard, Makkum, Friesland; the motor yacht Lady Ghislaine, later renamed Dancing Hare

stops.name: Manor Ground, Headington, the League Cup
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the League Cup and to 1985 for promotion; the day is the 1986 final date and is a reconstruction, not carried in the sources reached
stops.campa: He has taken over Oxford United when it was going under, and by 1985 he has it in the First Division, a club whose ground is squeezed between terraced houses a mile from his own front door. In April 1986 it wins the League Cup. The terraces sing that he is fat and round and never on the ground. He buys into Derby County the next year and has already bid for Manchester United, and none of it is a business. It is the part of the empire that cheers when he arrives.
suggested_refs: Oxford United at the Manor Ground, London Road, Headington, 1982-1987

stops.name: Holborn, the London Daily News
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of launch (February 1987) and of closure (July 1987); the day is a default
stops.campa: He launches the London Daily News, a round-the-clock paper for the capital, against the Evening Standard. Associated Newspapers relaunches the dead Evening News beneath his price and holds it there until he bleeds out. The paper closes in July, five months old, some twenty-five million pounds gone. In May of the same year his hostile bid for the American publisher Harcourt Brace Jovanovich is beaten off. He is losing money faster than the Pergamon journals can cover, and he keeps buying.
suggested_refs: The London Daily News, February to July 1987

stops.name: 866 Third Avenue, Macmillan bought
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He buys Macmillan Inc., the American publisher, for about 2.6 billion dollars, the largest thing he has ever done and the one that finally breaks the arithmetic. The price is paid with debt secured against assets whose value is asserted rather than tested. From this year the empire is a structure that must keep growing in order to keep standing, and every transaction afterwards, including the ones nobody is told about, is an attempt to hold the share price up until the next deal.
suggested_refs: The 1988 acquisition of Macmillan Inc., New York

stops.name: 220 East 42nd Street, the Daily News
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); month and day defaulted. An earlier draft of this research pinned the Daily News Building at -73.9738, two blocks west near Grand Central; that coordinate is rejected.
stops.campa: With the money from selling Pergamon he buys the New York Daily News, a failing tabloid in the great black building on East 42nd Street, at the exact moment his own group is being taken apart to pay interest. He is sixty-seven. He has sold the profitable thing that made him in order to buy an unprofitable thing that flatters him, and the photographers are there for it. Eight months remain. In London the pension fund transfers are already running, known to perhaps four people.
suggested_refs: The Daily News Building, 220 East 42nd Street, New York

segments.name: The Eastern Courts and the Israeli Connection

stops.name: Moscow, the flattering volumes
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the Soviet-bloc business dealings are general historical record; no specific Moscow visit date is confirmed in the sources reached. Year, month and day are all defaults within the decade.
stops.campa: He is one of the few Western businessmen who can get a Soviet appointment on request, and he trades on it: publishing deals with state houses, a series of interview volumes with world leaders including Mikhail Gorbachev, access sold back to Western governments as insight. British files later declassified record the Foreign Office assessing him in blunt terms. Nothing is proved and an assessment is not evidence. The file that holds it is not declassified until long after he is dead.
stops.quote: a thoroughly bad character and almost certainly financed by Russia
stops.quote_source: British Foreign Office internal assessment of Robert Maxwell, per Wikipedia's 'Robert Maxwell', drawing on later-declassified UK files. The original document was not located or read.
suggested_refs: The Pergamon 'Leaders of the World' interview volumes; declassified Foreign Office files on Maxwell

stops.name: Bucharest, the question to Ceausescu
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the Ceausescu courtship is general historical record and is not independently confirmed in the sources reached; the interview transcript was not located. Year, month and day are defaults within the decade.
stops.campa: His publishing houses produce authorised biographies of Eastern Bloc leaders and he conducts the interviews himself. The one with Nicolae Ceausescu becomes the specimen of the form. The opening question, widely quoted afterwards, asks the general secretary to account for his enormous popularity with the Romanian people, in a country where bread is queued for by candlelight. The books are not journalism and were never meant to be. They are the entry fee for access, and access is what he sells.
stops.quote: How do you account for your enormous popularity with the Romanian people?
stops.quote_source: Robert Maxwell's opening question to Nicolae Ceausescu, cited on Wikipedia's 'Robert Maxwell'. Not confirmed against the original interview transcript, which was not located.
suggested_refs: Pergamon's authorised biography of Nicolae Ceausescu

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the stake in Ma'ariv
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the Ma'ariv stake is reported elsewhere as bought in 1989 and sold to the Nimrodi family after his death, but the Wikipedia article on Maxwell does not mention Ma'ariv and the Ma'ariv article's ownership history does not mention Maxwell. Downgraded from [A] on that failure of attribution. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He acquires a stake in the Israeli daily Ma'ariv, one of a set of Israeli holdings and friendships built through the 1980s and sold on to the Nimrodi family after his death. He gives to Israeli causes, is received as a benefactor, and is on terms with the political and security establishment that no British proprietor before him has had. What passes in those rooms is not recorded anywhere that can be read. The closeness is documented; the content of it is not.
suggested_refs: Ma'ariv ownership history, 1989-1992; Maxwell's Israeli holdings

stops.name: London, the foreign editor sacked
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period (days before his death, autumn 1991); the day is a default and the canonical London pin stands for an unrecorded location
stops.campa: Ari Ben-Menashe, a former employee of Israeli military intelligence, tells journalists that Maxwell and the Daily Mirror foreign editor Nicholas Davies have both worked for Mossad for years, and that in 1986 Maxwell tipped the Israeli embassy to Mordechai Vanunu's nuclear disclosures. Vanunu had gone to the Sunday Times; a freelance then sold the story onward to the Sunday Mirror, which is Maxwell's. Maxwell calls the claims ludicrous and fires Davies. Nothing has ever been established.
stops.quote_source: Robert Maxwell on the Ben-Menashe allegations concerning Nicholas Davies, per Wikipedia's 'Robert Maxwell', which traces to Ben Laurance, John Hooper and David Sharrock, 'Maxwell's body found in sea', The Guardian, 6 November 1991.
suggested_refs: Ari Ben-Menashe, Profits of War (1992); the Vanunu affair, 1986

stops.name: House of Commons, named under privilege
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell')
stops.campa: George Galloway and Rupert Allason rise under parliamentary privilege and put the spy allegations on the record where no libel writ can reach them. Seymour Hersh repeats similar claims at a London press conference for The Samson Option; the Washington Post reports sources disputing him. The same literature places Adnan Khashoggi in the same traffic of arms, banks and services, a labelled node in Mark Lombardi's drawings. Maxwell has sued all his life. Fifteen days later he is dead.
suggested_refs: Hansard, House of Commons, 21 October 1991; Seymour Hersh, The Samson Option (1991)

stops.name: Amsterdam, Pergamon sold to Elsevier
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the sale and the price; [R] for the Amsterdam location, since no source reached confirms he went there in person. Month attested as March 1991; day defaulted.
stops.campa: To service debt he sells Pergamon Press and Maxwell Directories to Elsevier for 440 million pounds. Pergamon is the thing he built himself, the journals machine that paid for everything else, and it goes to a Dutch competitor in a forced sale forty years after Fitzroy Square. The proceeds are spent within months, part of them on a dying New York tabloid. Selling the engine to pay the interest leaves the debt in place and removes the income that was servicing it.
suggested_refs: The 1991 sale of Pergamon Press and Maxwell Directories to Elsevier

stops.name: Gibraltar Harbour, the voyage south
stops.date_confidence: [R]: press accounts of the final cruise commonly place the yacht at or past Gibraltar in late October 1991, and no source reached itemises the ports. The day is a default within that week.
stops.campa: The Lady Ghislaine leaves the Mediterranean and runs south for the Canaries with the owner aboard, out of reach of the telephone calls that are now the whole of his life. Fifty-one years earlier a refugee passed this rock going the other way, evacuating with a beaten exile army toward a country that had not yet given him a name. The ports of this last cruise are not itemised in anything reached here. The direction is certain, and the direction is away from London.
suggested_refs: Press reconstructions of the Lady Ghislaine's final voyage, autumn 1991
sources: General press reporting on the yacht's final route (unconfirmed in sources reached)

stops.name: Santa Cruz de Tenerife, the last islands
stops.date_confidence: [R]: Tenerife and Madeira are both commonly named in press accounts of the itinerary and neither is confirmed in the sources reached. The day is a default within the first days of November.
stops.campa: The yacht works through the Canaries in the first days of November, Tenerife and Madeira both named in press accounts and neither confirmed in any source reached. He is alone with the crew. In London the auditors are asking about the pension funds, the banks are asking about the collateral, and the Bank of England has asked for a meeting. He does not go. Ashore, hundreds of millions of pounds belonging to his own employees are missing, and almost nobody knows how much.
suggested_refs: Press reconstructions of the Canary Islands itinerary, 1-5 November 1991
sources: General press reporting (unconfirmed in sources reached)

stops.name: Off Gran Canaria, the last contact at 4:25
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the 4:25 a.m. last contact and the date. The position is contested: this research produced two coordinates for the same event, 28.4/-15.6 off Gran Canaria and 28.3/-16.5 south of Tenerife, about 90 km apart. The Gran Canaria reading is taken because the body was landed at Las Palmas; the conflict is recorded, not resolved. The argument with Kevin Maxwell is [R], not in the cited article.
stops.campa: On the night of the fourth he is in argument by telephone with his son Kevin over defaulted loans and the meeting in London he is refusing to attend. At 4:25 in the morning of the fifth he speaks to the crew of the Lady Ghislaine, and that is the last of him anyone records. In the morning he is not aboard. The yacht is making for Gran Canaria. A separate line of report puts the position ninety kilometres away, south of Tenerife, and the two accounts have never been reconciled.
suggested_refs: Inquest testimony of the Lady Ghislaine's crew, December 1991

stops.name: Puerto de la Luz, the body brought ashore
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell')
stops.campa: His body is recovered from the Atlantic naked and brought in to Las Palmas. Apart from a graze on the left shoulder there are no noticeable wounds on it. He is sixty-eight years old, with serious heart and lung disease. Spanish pathologists begin work the same day. The empire he leaves behind has a hole in it the size of the Mirror Group pensions, and for several more days nobody in the building at Holborn Circus knows that the hole is there at all.
suggested_refs: The recovery of Maxwell's body and its landing at Puerto de la Luz, 5 November 1991

stops.name: Las Palmas, the inquest
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); day defaulted. The proceeding was a Spanish judicial inquiry; an earlier draft of this research called it a 'coroner's court', which is an anglicism with no Spanish equivalent and is rejected.
stops.campa: Three pathologists examine him and cannot agree. In December the Spanish judicial inquiry rules that he died of a heart attack combined with accidental drowning. The judge rules out murder, and suicide is dismissed in effect rather than formally, which is the crack through which every subsequent argument has come. His son Ian says publicly that taking his own life was not in him. The timing, days before the fraud surfaced, is the fact nobody can make innocent and nobody can make criminal.
stops.quote: I think it is highly unlikely that he would have taken his own life, it wasn't in his makeup or his mentality
stops.quote_source: Ian Maxwell, 1991, per Wikipedia's 'Robert Maxwell'. An earlier draft of this research attributed the remark to Kevin Maxwell; that attribution is wrong.
suggested_refs: The December 1991 inquest at Las Palmas and the three pathologists' reports

stops.name: Mount of Olives, the state funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the day is carried by the interlock lens and is a reconstruction. Two coordinates for the cemetery appear in this research, 35.2427 and 35.2436, about ninety metres apart; the first is taken and the discrepancy recorded. The atlas canonical Temple Mount pin (31.778, 35.2354) is deliberately NOT inherited: the Mount of Olives is adjacent to it, not identical with it.
stops.campa: He is buried on the Mount of Olives, in the ground Jews have wanted above all others for three thousand years, at a funeral the State of Israel conducts for him. Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir attends. President Chaim Herzog gives the eulogy. At least six serving or former heads of the Israeli intelligence services are present, and his lawyer Samuel Pisar says the Kaddish at the graveside. No government has ever explained what a foreign newspaper proprietor did to earn that attendance.
suggested_refs: The Mount of Olives Jewish Cemetery, Jerusalem; press coverage of the funeral of 10 November 1991

stops.name: Holborn, the hole in the pension funds
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1991-1992 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Maxwell'); month and day defaulted. The comparisons to Banco Ambrosiano and First American are [R], structural parallels drawn from other atlas files and not asserted by any source as connection.
stops.campa: Within weeks the auditors find it: hundreds of millions of pounds taken from the pension funds of his own employees and used to buy Mirror Group shares and hold the price up. Pensioners face about half of what they were owed, before banks and government make part of it good. It is the shape of Roberto Calvi and Banco Ambrosiano ten years earlier in Licio Gelli's Italy, and of the secret ownership of First American that Clark Clifford was fronting in the same season in Washington.
suggested_refs: The Mirror Group pension fund investigations, 1991-1992

stops.name: London, the afterlives
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month for the memoir; the later items are attested to their years (1996, 1997, 2007, 2023) and are gathered under this pin rather than given separate ones
stops.campa: Elisabeth publishes A Mind of My Own in November 1994, the marriage told from inside by the woman who lived it. Joe Haines writes the other book. Jeffrey Archer builds The Fourth Estate around him and Rupert Murdoch in 1996; the Bond villain Elliot Carver is drawn from him in 1997; David Suchet plays him for the BBC in 2007 and wins an International Emmy; Roger Allam plays him in Tetris in 2023, bullying Gorbachev over a video game. Tom Bower's Maxwell: The Final Verdict appears in 1995. The last of these is made thirty-two years after his death.
stops.quote: one of the worst criminals of the century
stops.quote_source: George Galloway MP on Robert Maxwell, per Wikipedia's 'Robert Maxwell'. Not traced to a Hansard record or a dated interview in this research.
suggested_refs: Elisabeth Maxwell, A Mind of My Own (1994); Tom Bower, Maxwell: The Final Verdict (1995)

stops.name: Old Bailey, the sons acquitted
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1995-1996 for the trial and to 1992 for Kevin Maxwell's bankruptcy; the day is a reconstruction within the January 1996 verdict, and the Old Bailey coordinate is the standard Central Criminal Court pin
stops.campa: Kevin Maxwell is declared bankrupt with debts of about 400 million pounds. He and his brother Ian and two other directors stand trial for conspiracy to defraud over the pension money, and the jury acquits all of them unanimously. The money was taken and, in English law, nobody took it. The father who gave the instructions has been in the ground on the Mount of Olives for four years and cannot be put in the witness box, and the companies filed for bankruptcy protection in 1992.
suggested_refs: Regina v Maxwell and others, Central Criminal Court, 1995-1996

stops.name: Manhattan, the daughter in the dock
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the conviction; the arrest (July 2020) and sentence (28 June 2022) are attested to their dates. The courthouse coordinate is the Thurgood Marshall United States Courthouse and is a reconstruction, not carried in the sources reached.
stops.campa: Ghislaine Maxwell is arrested in July 2020, convicted on the twenty-ninth of December 2021 of sex trafficking offences connected to Jeffrey Epstein, and sentenced in June 2022 to twenty years. The reporting reaches back through her to her father: the yacht named for her, the money that vanished, the intelligence claims never proved and never disproved. No one has proposed opening the grave. The scrutiny arrives thirty years after the only inquest there will be.
suggested_refs: United States v. Ghislaine Maxwell, Southern District of New York, 2020-2022
